notes.body_html: Yoma 86b: “Reish Lakish said: Great is teshuvah, for willful sins become for him as inadvertent ones, as it says, ‘Return, Israel, unto Hashem your God, for you have stumbled [kashalta] in your iniquity’ (Hoshea 14:2) — ‘iniquity’ is willful, yet it is called a ‘stumbling’ [inadvertent]. But Reish Lakish [also] said: Great is teshuvah, for willful sins become for him as merits, as it says, ‘and when the wicked turns from his wickedness and does justice and righteousness, by them he shall live’ (Yechezkel 33:19)! — It is not difficult: here [merits] from love, there [inadvertent] from fear.” R’ Tzadok builds the whole siman on this ahavah/yirah distinction.

notes.body_html: Cf. the same distinction across Chassidus: Me’or Einayim (Ha’azinu) — teshuvah from fear renders willful sins “as inadvertent,” teshuvah from love renders them “as merits,” exactly R’ Tzadok’s yirah/ahavah frame; and Tanya, Likkutei Amarim ch. 7: “a teshuvah from a great love, from the depths of the heart, until the willful sins become like actual merits.”Chassidic and Maharal parallels — the mechanism of “z’donos as merits.” Maharal, Netivos Olam, Nesiv HaTeshuvah 2:17–19, explains that the sinner’s very distance becomes the measure of his later attachment: one who returns “from afar” displays a stronger deveikus, and therefore the z’don itself — the distance that he traversed — can be reckoned as a zechus. This closely complements R’ Tzadok’s claim here that teshuvah me-ahavah does not merely lighten the old act but reaches back to the will that generated it. Sefas Emes, Shabbos Shuvah 9:4, makes the distinction still more explicit: teshuvah from fear is awakened by the damage of sin and therefore weakens the sin into shogeg; teshuvah from love is awakened by longing to cleave to Torah and mitzvos, so that the sin itself becomes the cause of intensified love and added merit — “נמצא ממש זדונות נעשין כמו זכיות.” Tanya, Likkutei Amarim ch. 7, gives the same causal structure: because the soul had been “in a dry and shadowed land,” its later thirst for God is stronger, and “since through this he came to this great love,” the deliberate sins become actual merits. Shelah, Asarah Ma’amaros, Ma’amar Asiri §12, uses this distinction to reconcile the two statements about whether the baal teshuvah or the complete tzaddik is higher: ordinary teshuvah from fear does not surpass the tzaddik, whereas the rare teshuvah from love does. Chiddushei HaRim, Chayei Sarah §1, adds the temporal point that teshuvah can repair earlier days retroactively “as though he had performed mitzvos and good deeds” in them. These sources do not replace R’ Tzadok’s sharper metaphysical claim; they supply the devotional and conceptual mechanism by which the past itself becomes productive of present holiness.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Ohr Zarua LaTzadik §4): “this is the end-deed and this is the beginning-of-thought — Esav only said [it] in his heart, while Haman brought the decree out into act; and Kayin, and Gog and Magog, are likewise ‘the end-deed [that was] in thought first.’” This gives §5-1 its mechanism: every deed’s origin lies in the thought — “the end of the deed is in the thought first” — so when teshuvah “reaches the root of the soul in the mind,” it takes hold of the deed at its very beginning; the act that “already emerged into act” is rectified from the thought-root out of which it first came.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §1): “The ‘completion of the deed’ dwells in all the souls of Israel; and this is when his thought is bound day and night to the revealed [parts] of Torah and mitzvos, which is grasped by every Jew; and this ‘garment’ clothes also the ‘sealed thought’ that is above all — for all thoughts are only garments, except that this is more external and that more internal.” The se’if’s rectification: the heart’s teshuvah reaches up to the “sealed thought” — the root of the soul — and from there spreads down to the deeds.

notes.body_html: Nazir 23a: “One who intended to eat pork [basar chazir] and lamb came up in his hand [basar taleh] — even so he requires atonement and pardon”; the Gemara treats him like an inadvertent sinner as regards atonement, since he intended the forbidden. R’ Tzadok: teshuvah from fear leaves the deed “as inadvertent” — the intent to sin still needs atonement, though the act is no longer “willful.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §27): “willful sins as inadvertent ones means [they become] like mis’asek [one who acts with no intent at all], like a labor not needed for its own purpose.” This is §5-1’s “as inadvertent ones” made precise: teshuvah from fear does not erase the deed, but drains it of the intent that made it willful — so that what was done with full will is reckoned only as an unintended, purposeless act, a shogeg, the residue left once the sinful will is withdrawn.

notes.body_html: Yerushalmi Berachos 9:5: “עֲשֵׂה מֵאַהֲבָה וַעֲשֵׂה מִיִּרְאָה. עֲשֵׂה מֵאַהֲבָה — שֶׁאִם בָּאתָ לִשְׂנֹא, דַּע כִּי אַתָּה אוֹהֵב, וְאֵין אוֹהֵב שׂוֹנֵא. עֲשֵׂה מִיִּרְאָה — שֶׁאִם בָּאתָ לִבְעֹט, דַּע שֶׁאַתָּה יָרֵא, וְאֵין יָרֵא בּוֹעֵט” — “Serve from love and serve from fear. Serve from love — for if you come to hate, know that you are one who loves, and a lover does not hate. Serve from fear — for if you come to kick [rebel], know that you are one who fears, and one who fears does not kick.” This is the exact source (parallel in Yerushalmi Sotah 5:5): it stands in the sugya expounding “and you shall love Hashem your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” (on the Mishnah, “a person is obligated to bless over the bad as he blesses over the good”), the same passage that lists the “seven types of perushim” and crowns them with “the parush of love, like Avraham” (over against “the parush of fear, like Iyov”). Meforshim (Korban HaEidah, Pnei Moshe): fear is a real but lower rung — since fear restrains, one who genuinely fears will not “kick,” i.e. throw off the yoke. R’ Tzadok builds on this: fear can only still the heart from arousal to evil — “one who fears does not kick” — so it rectifies the deed (that the sin be reckoned only “as inadvertent,” not willful), but not the intent; the transformation of the past into outright merits belongs to love.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Chalomot §22): “a transgression for its own sake is greater than a mitzvah not for its own sake (Nazir 23b)… and through this the sins become [white] — the crimson turned to snow; and the victory [over Sisera] was through Devorah the prophetess.” This is §5-2’s very setting: the war against Sisera, God’s foe, was won by the power of aveirah lishmah — the deed that, done wholly for Heaven, outweighs a lukewarm mitzvah — the same power by which “the willful become as merits,” the crimson sins made white.Izhbitz on exceptional action and the limits of bechirah. Mei HaShiloach I, Pinchas §2, is an unusually close — and deliberately dangerous — parallel to the category R’ Tzadok is discussing. The Izhbitzer distinguishes levels in which a person progressively exhausts his ability to escape a temptation, culminating in a case where, after genuine resistance, he understands the event as bound up with a hidden Divine will; he applies this to Zimri while simultaneously presenting Pinchas’s opposite judgment as valid and accepted by Heaven. The point is therefore not a prospective license to transgress. On the contrary, the passage dramatizes how little a person can know, before the fact, whether he has truly reached such a boundary of bechirah. This sharpens R’ Tzadok’s treatment of Yael, Esther, and Shimshon: an aveirah lishmah is not the ordinary suspension of halachah by subjective inspiration, but an extreme case of self-surrender in which personal benefit is absent and the actor is prepared even to bear punishment. The Izhbitz parallel is especially useful here because it places the question precisely at the fault-line between human choice and the hidden Divine ordering that can be recognized, if at all, only after the deed has been fully clarified.

notes.body_html: Shimshon and the Plishtim — background: Shimshon (Shoftim chs. 13–16), of the tribe of Dan, was the last of the great Shoftim and a nazir from the womb (his mother so instructed by the angel), of whom it was foretold “he shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Plishtim.” The Plishtim were Israel’s dominant oppressors in his day, and his superhuman strength was bound up with his uncut Nazirite hair. He judged Israel twenty years; Delilah, at the Plishtim chieftains’ bidding, drew out his secret; they seized him, put out his eyes, and bound him to grind in the prison-house at Azzah (Gaza). At the temple of their god Dagon, his hair regrown, he prayed “remember me and strengthen me only this once,” grasped the two central pillars, and cried “tamos nafshi im Plishtim — let my soul die with the Plishtim” (Shoftim 16:30), bringing the house down upon the assembled lords — “so that the dead he slew at his death were more than those he slew in his life.” On this the Sages (Sotah 9b–10a) expound his whole career, and rule that “Shimshon judged Israel like the Father in Heaven.” R’ Tzadok reads “tamos nafshi” at its depth: Shimshon feared he might be judged a me’abed atzmo la-da’as (one who knowingly takes his own life, who forfeits even his share in the World to Come) — for he died to avenge himself and slay God’s enemies, not to save his soul from sin or to save Israel — yet out of sheer love for God, to prevent the chillul Hashem of his capture, he consented even to that.

notes.body_html: Berachos 34b: the sugya of bowing (keri’ah) in Shemoneh Esrei. The Mishnah teaches that a commoner bows at “Modim” and at “Baruch Atah Hashem” of the first berachah; the Gemara (34a–b) adds the gradations of rank: a Kohen Gadol bows at the end of every berachah, “and a king, once he has bowed, does not straighten up until he completes his entire prayer” (מֶלֶךְ כֵּיוָן שֶׁכָּרַע שׁוּב אֵינוֹ זוֹקֵף עַד שֶׁגּוֹמֵר כָּל תְּפִלָּתוֹ). Rashi: the more exalted one’s station, the more constant the submission (hachna’ah) required of him before the King of kings. R’ Tzadok takes this as the emblem of kingship = the intensity of fear and submission: the king, once bowed, never straightens — unremitting hachna’ah. Hence David, whose middah is malchus / Gevurah, could not merely subdue the yetzer (which leaves it standing, ready to rise) but was compelled to kill it outright.

This is the classic scriptural enumeration of the seven lower middos/sefiros (Gedulah = Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferes, Netzach, Hod, “ki chol” = Yesod, and ha-mamlachah = Malchus). notes.body_html: Yeshayah 41:2: “מִי הֵעִיר מִמִּזְרָח, צֶדֶק יִקְרָאֵהוּ לְרַגְלוֹ, יִתֵּן לְפָנָיו גּוֹיִם וּמְלָכִים יַרְדְּ, יִתֵּן כֶּעָפָר חַרְבּוֹ כְּקַשׁ נִדָּף קַשְׁתּוֹ” — “Who roused one from the east, calling righteousness to his feet? He delivers up nations before him and makes him tread down kings; his sword makes them as dust, his bow as driven chaff.” From Yeshayah’s prophecy of consolation (ch. 41), in which God summons the nations to judgment and asks “who aroused [he’ir]” the victor from the east. Rashi and the Sages apply “mi he’ir mimizrach” to Avraham — whom God “roused” from the east (Ur Kasdim / Aram), “calling righteousness to his feet,” and before whom He delivered up the four kings (Bereishis 14). R’ Tzadok reads the verb “he’ir” as the point: it was God who first aroused Avraham — Avraham’s light shining “out of the darkness” came not by his own initiative but by God’s love preceding him, the “arousal from Above” (is’aruta di-le’eila) that always precedes love. (The received text reads Yeshayah 41:2.)

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Sichas Shedim §1): “when a person is made whole [in the middah of Yaakov], the Holy One calls him ‘My twin [te’omasi]’ — that both are equal; and ‘He did not budge from cherishing her until He called her My mother’ — as though she were even greater than He, generating, as it were, the beginning-of-thought that is His.” This is §5-6’s astonishing claim exactly: love needs equals, and God Himself confers the equality — calling Knesses Yisrael “My twin,” then raising her past even that, to “My mother,” so that the love has its “like” on both sides.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §24): “One [greets] his fellow out of love and joining; but fear is from the side of ‘derech eretz’ toward a man who is great and separate from him. And by Hashem, both are together, and one without the other does not suffice — for fear alone brings folly (‘is not your fear your folly?’), and joy alone brings frivolity.” The se’if’s point: fear, unlike love, is not between equals — it is toward “one great and separate,” who “casts and gives the dread.”

notes.body_html: “When He does judgment on the wicked He is feared”: R’ Tzadok cites in brief the established teaching that God’s awe is made manifest through judgment. Its scriptural anchor is “nora Elokim mi-mikdashecha” (Tehillim 68:36), which the Sages expound, “read not mi-mikdashecha (from Your sanctuary) but mi-mekudashecha (through those You sanctify [in executing judgment])” (Zevachim 115b; and cf. the Zohar, that when the Holy One performs judgment “He is exalted and held in awe”). R’ Tzadok’s use: the arousal of Gevurah above (the doing of din) is precisely what begets fear in the human heart; yet, unlike love, “the middah is not the same in both” — the One feared and the one who fears are not equals — so this is not called “an arousal from Above that precedes an arousal from below.”

notes.body_html: Iyov 41:3: “מִי הִקְדִּימַנִי וַאֲשַׁלֵּם, תַּחַת כָּל הַשָּׁמַיִם לִי הוּא” — “Who has preceded Me, that I should repay him? Whatever is under the whole heaven is Mine.” From God’s answer to Iyov out of the whirlwind (the Livyasan passage, ch. 41), asserting His absolute sovereignty. Rashi: who has come before Me [with a gift or a merit] that I should owe him repayment — for everything under the heavens is already Mine. The Sages apply “mi hikdimani va-ashalem” to the mitzvos: none can “precede” God and put Him in his debt, since He Himself first provides the very means of the mitzvah (a house before its mezuzah, a garment before its tzitzis — Vayikra Rabbah 27:2, and the like). R’ Tzadok’s use: even fear is not purely from the person’s own side — “who has preceded Me?” — for God Himself precedes to bring him the thing that rouses fear; yet it is still called “an arousal from below,” since (unlike love) that thing does not rouse “in clear act.”

notes.body_html: Yeshayah 8:21: “וְעָבַר בָּהּ נִקְשֶׁה וְרָעֵב, וְהָיָה כִי יִרְעַב וְהִתְקַצַּף וְקִלֵּל בְּמַלְכּוֹ וּבֵאלֹהָיו וּפָנָה לְמָעְלָה” — “And he shall pass through it hard-pressed and hungry; and it shall be, when he is hungry, that he grows furious and curses his king and his god, and turns his face upward.” From Yeshayah’s prophecy of the darkness overtaking those who will not heed “to Torah and to testimony” (ch. 8). Rashi: the one in distress, rather than turning to God, “curses his king” (his ruler) “and his god” (his idol) and rails upward. R’ Tzadok’s use: this typifies the lower fear of the nations — when the middah of Gevurah and wrath is aroused in them, it does not draw them to submission but to the reverse: they “strengthen themselves” and rebel (the dross of Gevurah) — as against those in Israel who “desire to fear His Name” and “search like buried treasures” for the fear of God.

notes.body_html: Nechemyah 1:11: “אָנָּא אֲדֹנָי, תְּהִי נָא אָזְנְךָ קַשֶּׁבֶת אֶל תְּפִלַּת עַבְדְּךָ וְאֶל תְּפִלַּת עֲבָדֶיךָ הַחֲפֵצִים לְיִרְאָה אֶת שְׁמֶךָ […] וְאֲנִי הָיִיתִי מַשְׁקֶה לַמֶּלֶךְ” — “Please, O Lord, let Your ear be attentive to the prayer of Your servant and the prayer of Your servants who desire to fear Your Name…” The verse closes Nechemyah’s opening prayer (ch. 1), as he steels himself to approach the Persian king; he characterizes the faithful as “ha-chafeitzim le-yirah es shemecha” — those whose very desire is to attain the fear of God. notes.body_html: Mishlei 2:4–5: “אִם תְּבַקְשֶׁנָּה כַכָּסֶף, וְכַמַּטְמוֹנִים תַּחְפְּשֶׂנָּה. אָז תָּבִין יִרְאַת ה׳, וְדַעַת אֱלֹקִים תִּמְצָא” — “If you seek it like silver and search it out like buried treasures, then you will understand the fear of Hashem and find the knowledge of God.” From Shlomo’s exhortation (Mishlei 2) that wisdom and the fear of God are won only by strenuous search. Meforshim: yiras Hashem is not given passively — one must “dig” for it as for hidden treasure. R’ Tzadok’s use: precisely because fear must be sought out — “search like buried treasures” — it is “an arousal from below,” the striving of the person; and this is the whole matter of the Torah, which issues from the side of Gevurah, commanding a person to labor to choose the good.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §186): “Then Avraham and Yitzchak were united together, as it says ‘now I know that you fear God’ — and this is like ‘R’ Chisda and R’ Sheshes’ (Eruvin 67a), two opposites, R’ Chisda ‘sharp’ and R’ Sheshes ‘Sinai,’ each ‘trembling’ before the other — that is the fear; and through the ‘sharpening,’ the God-fearing ones spoke and were joined and included [one in the other].” Exactly the se’if: after the Akeidah, Avraham was “included in the middah of Yitzchak” — fear.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §10): “the [modes of] service are love, fear, and deveikus; love and fear are the two wings and the two arms of the world — and they are the two Avos, Avraham and Yitzchak; and deveikus is ‘the one who grasps the body of the King,’ the form of Yaakov engraved on the Throne.” This is the structure behind §5-8’s “now I know that you fear God”: love and fear are the two wings on which one rises, and neither flies alone — so Avraham’s love reached its height only when, at the Akeidah, it was joined to Yitzchak’s fear, the two wings become one.

notes.body_html: Yeshayah 26:12: “ה׳ תִּשְׁפֹּת שָׁלוֹם לָנוּ, כִּי גַּם כָּל מַעֲשֵׂינוּ פָּעַלְתָּ לָּנוּ” — “Hashem, You will establish peace for us, for You have also wrought all our deeds for us.” From the “song” of the future redemption sung in the land of Yehudah (Yeshayah 26). Meforshim (Rashi, Radak): all that we have accomplished, You have wrought for us — every good deed of ours is ultimately God’s own doing. R’ Tzadok’s use: the ultimate rectification (through Mashiach) requires the removal of “striving” and the revelation that “gam kol ma’aseinu pa’alta lanu” — all is from Him; and then even the past sins turn to merits, for the “distancings” themselves were, in truth, His drawings-near.Izhbitz-Radzin and Ger on the future revelation that “all our deeds You wrought for us.” Mei HaShiloach II, Zechariah 4:1, reads “לא בחיל ולא בכח כי אם ברוחי” as the future state in which the powers of human action are progressively effaced and the inheritance of Yaakov is revealed: Yaakov describes himself as one who does nothing, even in the smallest matter, until God “takes him by the hand and leads him like sheep after the shepherd.” That is a striking complement to R’ Tzadok’s use of Yeshayah 26:12 here: the final repair comes when the very framework of self-authored hishtadlus is removed and it is disclosed that “all is from Him.” Chiddushei HaRim, Vayigash §2, states the same point retrospectively: at the complete redemption it will be seen “למפרע שכל עניני הגלות היה לטובתינו,” and every detail of the exile will be clarified as part of the good; he therefore describes the descent itself as carrying its ascent within it, “אנכי ארד עמך… אעלך גם עלה.” These are not denials of the Torah’s present demand for bechirah; they describe the eschatological disclosure R’ Tzadok is speaking about — what becomes visible only when the work of human striving has reached its end.

notes.body_html: Niddah 31b: “Why did the Torah say [a niddah is impure] seven days? Because [a husband] becomes habituated to his wife and repelled by her; therefore the Torah said she is impure seven days, so that she be beloved to him as on the day of her wedding.” R’ Tzadok: love renewed after distance is greater — so teshuvah from love makes the very sins (the “distance”) the cause of a greater nearness, i.e. “merits.”Maharal — distance itself can generate a stronger return. Maharal, Nesiv HaTeshuvah 2:17–19, gives a conceptual analogue to R’ Tzadok’s use of the niddah interval: the one who comes to God “from afar” can reveal a more forceful attachment than one who was never distant, just as fire far below moves upward toward its natural place with greater force. Maharal therefore says that the sin, which was itself the distance, becomes a merit when that very distance is what reveals the depth of the return. R’ Tzadok develops the same principle here in relational language: the separation makes the renewed nearness more beloved, and so the z’donos themselves become the causes of kiruv.

notes.body_html: Shabbos 30a: the Gemara recounts that David said before the Holy One, “mechol li al oso avon — pardon me for that sin,” and He answered, “machul lach — it is pardoned you.” David then asked, “asei imi os be-chayai — make a sign [of the pardon] in my lifetime,” and He replied, “be-chayecha eini modia — in your lifetime I will not make it known; be-chayei Shlomo bincha ani modia — in the lifetime of Shlomo your son I will make it known.” (This was borne out when the Temple gates clung shut until Shlomo invoked “zochrah le-chasdei David avdecha,” whereupon all knew the Holy One had pardoned him.) R’ Tzadok’s use: even David, who returned from complete love, was told “in your lifetime I will not make known” — for “do not awaken love until it desires”: the influx of love descends only when its time has “desired,” and it is not in a person’s power to compel it by striving; yet David, by his very request, “brought himself near.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Peri Tzadik, Tetzaveh §3): “It is because the Holy One chose him and sanctified him, as [expounded] on ‘happy is Aharon, whom [God] chose and drew near’; and therefore ‘the lips of a kohen guard knowledge’ — for the crown [of kehunah] is external, but inwardly ‘knowledge fills his place.’” Exactly the se’if: Aharon was “chosen and brought near” — he did not bring himself near by striving.Sefas Emes on Aharon’s shame — “for this you were chosen.” Sefas Emes, Shemini 7:3, directly interprets Rashi’s “קרב אל המזבח — למה אתה בוש? לכך נבחרת” through the same axis as this se’if. He distinguishes בחירה, the standing of the complete tzaddik, from קריבה, the drawing-near of the baal teshuvah, and writes that Aharon certainly returned from love, so that even deliberate sins become merits — all the more an inadvertent participation in the Calf. He goes further: it is close to say that Aharon’s very connection to that sin was arranged so that he could elevate the teshuvah of Klal Yisrael into teshuvah from love; thus “לכך נבחרת” means that precisely through repairing the fall into zechus, his kiruv itself becomes a form of bechirah. This is almost a direct Chassidic commentary on R’ Tzadok’s paradox here: what appeared to disqualify Aharon from avodah became the very ground of his being chosen and brought near.

notes.body_html: Yisro, Rachav, and Aharon — background: the se’if turns on two Talmudic categories (from Bamidbar Rabbah 3:2, cited in §8): “kervu aval lo bacharu” (brought near but not chosen) and “bacharu ve-kervu” (chosen and brought near). Yisro (Shemos 18) was the Midyanite priest and Moshe’s father-in-law; hearing of the splitting of the sea and the war with Amalek, he came to the wilderness, converted, and gave the counsel for the system of judges — his “nearness” arising by circumstance (being Moshe’s father-in-law), not by his own striving. Rachav (Yehoshua 2) was the innkeeper of Yericho who sheltered the two spies, declared “Hashem your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below,” was spared at the city’s fall, and converted; the Sages (Megillah 14b) say she married Yehoshua and became ancestress of prophets and priests — her “nearness,” too, came by circumstance (the spies who lodged in her house). Both are “brought near but not chosen”: converts, whose initial drawing-near is God’s doing, though afterward striving is needed. Aharon alone, in this world, is “chosen and brought near” — chosen for the avodah without striving; and R’ Tzadok’s paradox is that he merited it through the shame of the Golden Calf, “for the Holy One uses only broken vessels”: as the Midrash (Toras Kohanim / Vayikra Rabbah, Shemini) records, Moshe said to the abashed Aharon, “lamah atah bosh? le-kach nivcharta — why are you ashamed? for this you were chosen.”

notes.body_html: Nazir 3a / Taanis 11a; Tosafos, Nazir 19b–20b: R’ Elazar HaKappar holds a nazirite is a “sinner” (for afflicting himself from wine — “and he shall atone for him, for he sinned against the soul,” Bamidbar 6:11), and a fortiori one who afflicts himself by fasting; yet Scripture also calls the nazirite “fitting [na’eh].” Tosafos reconciles: he is both — the mitzvah outweighs the sin (so “fitting”), yet a trace of “sin” remains (so atonement is needed). R’ Tzadok: so too the baal teshuvah’s past — a merit that yet leaves residual “shame,” until the future reveals it as pure merit. (Developed further in Siman 10.)

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §34): “in truth it is hidden and concealed — ‘the sin of Israel shall be sought and be no more, for I shall forgive’ — this is [so] only in Israel, whose sins are ‘like the [scarlet] threads’ set in order [from the six days of creation]… and they have a good fragrance from afar.” This is §5-11 precisely: in this world the merit hidden within the sin is “not revealed and clear to the eye,” concealed like a fragrance sensed only “from afar” — but at the end “the sin shall be sought and be no more,” disclosed to all as no sin at all.Izhbitz-Radzin on what is visible only after complete teshuvah. Sod Yesharim, Parashas Parah 2:1–2, draws a precise distinction between the sinner’s responsibility before teshuvah and the Divine disclosure afterward. From the human side, repentance clarifies that at the hour of sin his דעת was absent — like a body severed from its head — and he must attribute the deficiency to himself. But after complete teshuvah, when z’donos become zechuyos, Hashem can illuminate that the very act which had appeared dark was never outside the supernal will: “אותו הפעולה בעצמה… היתה נמי גם אז מלא אור.” The work insists on the sequence: first the person owns the failure and returns; only afterward is the deeper Divine connection disclosed. This maps closely onto R’ Tzadok’s distinction here between this world, where the former act still carries shame and cannot yet be seen with complete clarity, and the future, when it will be revealed that the apparent distance itself was a form of nearness. Beis Yaakov, Vayigash 11:1–3, develops the same point through the image of Torah as “living words”: after a person returns with his whole heart, he can see retroactively that what he passed through was encompassed within divrei Elokim chayim, and the earlier meaning of his history is “healed.” Again, this is a retrospective illumination granted by teshuvah, not a heter to define a prohibited act in advance as God’s will.

notes.body_html: Berachos 34b: When R’ Chanina ben Dosa prayed for R’ Yochanan ben Zakkai’s sick son and he recovered, R’ Yochanan said, “Had ben Zakkai stuck his head between his knees all day, they would not have heeded him.” His wife asked, “Is Chanina greater than you?” He answered, “No — but he is like a servant before the King [who may enter at any time], while I am like a minister before the King [admitted only at set times].” R’ Tzadok: the “service” (prayer, “standing before the King”) is itself the nearness in which one sees that all is merit — and God is nearest to the broken, anxious heart.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §17): “After the teshuvah and rectification, that willful sins become merits — behold the people of Shushan, who ‘added’ in the sin of the [second] feast (which was in Shushan alone), and so there was added to them the merit of vengeance from their enemies one more day; and such is the measure: after they rectified their sin, judgment reached to slay those nations, where there had been a chillul Hashem.” The se’if’s “willful sins and merits” attained in this world — as with the people of Shushan.Mei HaShiloach — why the baal teshuvah can stand higher. Mei HaShiloach II, Berachos 34b, reconciles the opposing statements about tzaddikim and baalei teshuvah by separating body from soul: the complete tzaddik possesses the more purified body, but the baal teshuvah’s nefesh is hewn from a higher place. He explains that in the future, when deliberate sins become merits, Hashem will show the baal teshuvah that through his cry of teshuvah he touched an “עומק עמוק מכל דעת שהאדם יכול להשיג.” This is an especially close complement to R’ Tzadok’s language here: in this world the merit concealed in the old sin is not yet fully visible; the future disclosure is not that sin ceased to have been sin from the human standpoint, but that the baal teshuvah’s broken-hearted return reaches a depth that the earlier, unbroken state could not reveal.

notes.body_html: The sefiros — background: Kabbalah counts ten sefiros (divine “attributes” or channels): Keser, Chochmah, Binah; then the seven “lower” sefiros — Chesed (loving-kindness / expansion), Gevurah (might / din / contraction), Tiferes (harmony); Netzach (eternity / victory), Hod (splendor / radiance), Yesod (foundation); and Malchus (kingship / the nukva, the receiving side). R’ Tzadok maps the rungs of teshuvah onto these middos, this fifth rung standing over-against Hod. He defines Hod as the ziv (radiance) that spreads from the essence of Gevurah: Gevurah “contracts” the King’s glory (so that it is not in free expansion like Chesed), and from that contraction only the radiance — Hod — is revealed. Thus as fear (yirah) spreads from Gevurah, so shame (bushah) — “a branch of fear” — spreads from Hod. (In the standard scheme Netzach and Hod are the “two thighs” from which the prophets are nourished — Moshe corresponding to Netzach and Aharon to Hod, as the next se’if develops.) A parallel development in R’ Tzadok’s own writings — on Hod, bushah, and the “whitening of the face” — is given in the corpus note on this se’if.

notes.body_html: Daniel 5:6: “אֱדַיִן מַלְכָּא זִיוֺהִי שְׁנוֹהִי, וְרַעְיֹנֹהִי יְבַהֲלוּנֵּהּ, וְקִטְרֵי חַרְצֵהּ מִשְׁתָּרַיִן, וְאַרְכֻבָּתֵהּ דָּא לְדָא נָקְשָׁן” — “then the king’s radiance was changed, and his thoughts alarmed him; the joints of his loins were loosened, and his knees knocked one against the other.” The scene is Belshatzar’s feast (Daniel 5): the Babylonian king drank from the sacred vessels plundered from the Beis HaMikdash, whereupon a hand wrote upon the wall “mene mene tekel u-farsin,” and his face blanched in terror. Sefas Emes, Shemini 7:3, connects Aharon’s own teshuvah from love with the elevation of the entire people’s return, invoking “על כל פשעים תכסה אהבה.” Read beside Avos’ “אוהב את הבריות ומקרבן לתורה,” the two teachings illuminate one another: Aharon’s mode of kiruv is itself the logic of teshuvah me-ahavah. Love precedes the sinner’s shame; the shame then makes him abandon the sin; and the very path by which he had been distant becomes the cause of a deeper return. This fits R’ Tzadok’s point that in Aharon’s middah the z’donos become zechuyos specifically because the Divine or human love shown to the sinner is what produces the new nearness.

notes.body_html: Eichah 1:13: “מִמָּרוֹם שָׁלַח אֵשׁ בְּעַצְמֹתַי וַיִּרְדֶּנָּה […] נְתָנַנִי שֹׁמֵמָה, כָּל הַיּוֹם דָּוָה” — “from on high He sent fire into my bones and it prevailed; […] He has made me desolate and faint [daveh] all the day.” From the first kinah of Eichah, Yirmeyahu’s lament over the Churban, in the voice of stricken Jerusalem. Meforshim: “daveh” is languishing, sick — the faintness likened to the davah of niddah. R’ Tzadok’s use: “kol ha-yom daveh” alludes to the fifth millennium, the “day” wholly given over to exile, which corresponds to Hod — for in reverse of letters “Hod” (ה־ו־ד) is “Daveh” (ד־ו־ה); the languishing distance of exile is, like the niddah of a wife, a distancing that is ultimately for a drawing-near of love.

notes.body_html: Daniel 10:8: “וַאֲנִי נִשְׁאַרְתִּי לְבַדִּי, וָאֶרְאֶה אֶת הַמַּרְאָה הַגְּדֹלָה הַזֹּאת, וְלֹא נִשְׁאַר בִּי כֹּחַ, וְהוֹדִי נֶהְפַּךְ עָלַי לְמַשְׁחִית, וְלֹא עָצַרְתִּי כֹּחַ” — “and I alone was left, and I saw this great vision, and no strength remained in me; my Hod was turned within me to ruin, and I retained no strength.” From Daniel’s final vision (ch. 10) by the river Chidekel, where an angel comes to reveal “what shall befall your people in the end of days” — the succession of kingdoms, Yavan (Greece) and Edom (Rome) among them. Meforshim (Rashi, Ibn Ezra): overwhelmed by the vision, Daniel’s bodily hod — the fresh glow of the face — drained away to “ruin.” R’ Tzadok reads “ve-hodi nehpach alai le-mashchis” of the middah of Hod: the very turning of Hod into daveh foretold by the vision — the ruin of the Hod and radiance of Knesses Yisrael through the exiles of Greece and Rome (“Hod” reversed being “Daveh”).

notes.body_html: Bereishis 27:40: “וְעַל חַרְבְּךָ תִחְיֶה וְאֶת אָחִיךָ תַּעֲבֹד, וְהָיָה כַּאֲשֶׁר תָּרִיד וּפָרַקְתָּ עֻלּוֹ מֵעַל צַוָּארֶךָ” — “and by your sword you shall live, and you shall serve your brother; but it shall be, when you are aggrieved [tarid], that you will break his yoke from off your neck.” This is the blessing Yitzchak gave Esav, after Yaakov had received the primary blessing (ch. 27). Rashi: “al charbecha — by your sword you shall live”; Esav’s portion is the way of the sword and plunder; and “when you are aggrieved” — when Israel transgresses the Torah, Esav is given license to cast off his subjugation and dominate. R’ Tzadok’s use: “by your sword you shall live” brands Esav (and his seed, Rome) as the dross of Gevurah — the way of the sword — the very reverse of Aharon’s Hod, “who loved peace and pursued peace.”

notes.body_html: Shabbos 17a: the Gemara (on Mishnah Shabbos 1:4) recounts the “eighteen matters [shemoneh esrei davar]” enacted in the attic of Chananyah ben Chizkiyah ben Garon, on the day the vote went to Beis Shammai when they outnumbered Beis Hillel — a day the Gemara treats gravely (“as hard for Israel as the day the Calf was made”). Tosafos (with the Tosefta and Yerushalmi Shabbos 1:4) records the dispute of R’ Eliezer and R’ Yehoshua whether that day was for good — that “they heaped up the measure” of Torah — or for ill — that “they wiped away the measure” through an excess of stringencies. R’ Tzadok’s use: Hillel and his house did not favor a multitude of safeguards (Beis Hillel rule leniently); once Matisyahu “repaired the Hod” and the rung that rectifies the past shone forth, a proliferation of fences-going-forward was no longer needed.

notes.body_html: Menachos 29b: Moshe saw R’ Akiva expounding “heaps of laws” from the crowns of the letters, then saw R’ Akiva’s flesh “weighed out in the market” [his martyrdom]. “He said: Master of the Universe, this is Torah and this is its reward? He said: Be silent — so it arose in [My] thought [kach alah be-machashavah lefanai].” Berachos 61b: as they raked R’ Akiva’s flesh with iron combs at the hour of Kerias Shema, he accepted the yoke of Heaven, saying, “All my days I was troubled by this verse, ‘with all your soul’ — even if He takes your soul — I said, when will it come to my hand that I may fulfill it? And now that it has come, shall I not fulfill it?” He prolonged “Echad” until his soul departed. R’ Tzadok: the martyrs clarified that death can be “without sin” — a merit or a kivshei d’Rachmana — and, since “the yetzer hara is the Angel of Death” (Bava Basra 16a), so too a sin can be, at root, God’s own will — hence “merits.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Likkutei Maamarim §5): “‘if the sins be as scarlet [ka-shanim]’ — which are ordered and come from the six days of creation — ‘like snow they shall whiten,’ and there is no sin here at all; and the root of all the sins is ‘if you walk with Me b’keri,’ that you reckon everything as happenstance.” This is §5-18’s “so it arose in thought before Him”: the willful sins were set within God’s primordial ordering from the six days, so they whiten to “no sin at all” — merits; while the true root of sin is the reverse, treating the world as mikreh rather than His will.
